solution:
Column II is the form of energy that the source in column I supplies, and column III is the plant that uses it. Re-paired:

| I | II | III |
|---|---|---|
| Coal | Thermal Energy | Thermal plant |
| Uranium | Nuclear Energy | Nuclear power plant |
| Water Reservoir | Potential energy | Hydro electric plant |
| Wind | Kinetic Energy | Wind electricity plant |

Every pairing is stated in the chapter. **Coal** is burnt in a boiler and the water is turned to steam "using the thermal energy released due to burning of coal", in what the chapter calls a thermal power plant. **Uranium** appears as the fuel of the nuclear power plant, where "the energy released by fission of nuclei of atoms like Uranium or Plutonium is used to generate the steam". In the **water reservoir** of a hydroelectric plant "the potential energy in water stored in dam is converted into kinetic energy of water". And of **wind** the chapter says "the kinetic energy in wind has been used since long", the wind turbine being "the machine which converts the kinetic energy of wind to electrical energy".

**Coal** is the fuel used in a thermal power plant. The chapter describes the boiler heating water "using the thermal energy released due to burning of coal" to raise steam of very high temperature and pressure.

The chapter lists three problems with this way of generating power:

1. **Air pollution due to burning of coal.** Burning coal emits gases like carbon dioxide, sulphur oxide and nitrogen oxide, "which are harmful to the health".
2. **Soot particles.** Along with those gases, soot particles are released into the environment, and these "may cause serious health problems related to the respiratory system".
3. **Limited reserves.** "The reserves of fuel used in this method i.e. coal are limited. Therefore, in future, there will be limitations on the availability of the coal."

The chapter's later section on generation and the environment adds that the rising percentage of carbon dioxide is linked to global warming and that nitrogen dioxide leads to acid rain.

Besides the thermal power plant, the chapter describes two other plants that pass through a **thermal energy** stage:

- **Nuclear power plant** -- the thermal energy comes from **nuclear fission**. "The energy released by fission of nuclei of atoms like Uranium or Plutonium is used to generate the steam of high temperature and high pressure." Its energy chain begins Nuclear energy \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy.
- **Solar thermal power plant** -- the thermal energy comes from **solar radiation**. "Many reflectors reflect and concentrate solar radiation on absorbers. There solar energy is converted into heat energy. Using this heat energy steam is generated to drive the turbine and generator."

So the thermal energy is obtained in three different ways across the three plants: by **burning coal** (thermal plant), by **nuclear fission of uranium or plutonium** (nuclear plant), and by **concentrating sunlight on an absorber** (solar thermal plant). In each case the thermal energy is used for the same purpose -- to raise high-pressure steam that drives a turbine coupled to a generator.

**Worth noting about the natural-gas plant:** it does burn a fuel, but the chapter's own flow chart for it (figure 5.13) runs Chemical energy in natural gas \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy generated due to combustion \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy, with no thermal-energy stage named. On the chapter's own labelling it is therefore not counted here.

Counting from the chapter's own energy-transformation flow charts:

| Power generation | Chain of energy forms | Conversions |
|---|---|---|
| Thermal (fig 5.6) | Chemical (coal) \(\rightarrow\) Thermal \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 4 |
| Nuclear (fig 5.9) | Nuclear \(\rightarrow\) Thermal \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 4 |
| Solar thermal | Solar \(\rightarrow\) Thermal \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 4 |
| Natural gas (fig 5.13) | Chemical (gas) \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic from combustion \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 3 |
| Hydroelectric (fig 5.16) | Potential \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in flowing water \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 3 |
| Wind (fig 5.21) | Kinetic in wind \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 2 |
| Solar photovoltaic | Solar \(\rightarrow\) Electrical | 1 |

**Maximum:** the **thermal, nuclear and solar thermal** plants, each with five energy forms and four conversions. They share the whole tail of the chain -- thermal energy, steam, turbine, generator -- and differ only in where the thermal energy comes from.

**Minimum:** the **solar photovoltaic** cell, with a single conversion. The chapter makes the point explicitly: "electrical energy can be generated directly from solar radiation without using generator and without using the principle of electromagnetic induction. This happens in solar photovoltaic cells. Solar photovoltaic cells convert the solar energy directly into electrical energy."

**Note:** the chapter prints an energy-form flow chart for the thermal, nuclear, natural-gas, hydroelectric and wind plants, but not for the solar thermal plant -- its figure 5.29 on printed p58 is a chain of components (concentrators, absorber, steam turbine, electric generator), so the solar thermal row above follows the pattern of the other thermal plants rather than a printed chart.

**Thermal.**

The chapter's "Do you know?" table of energy sources used for electrical power generation gives India's shares as coal 60, natural gas 08, hydroelectric 14, nuclear energy 02, petroleum 0.3 and renewable sources 15.7 per cent. Coal is much the largest, and coal is burnt in what the chapter calls a **thermal power plant** -- "In thermal power plants, the chemical energy in the coal is converted into electrical energy".

The printed crossword grid allows seven letters here, which rules out the tempting four-letter answer "coal" and confirms **thermal**.

**Wind.**

The chapter groups "water-reservoir, wind, sunlight, biofuel" together as sources that "are never-ending i.e are perpetual", and its own "Do you know?" table has a row headed "Renewable sources (wind, solar etc.)".

The clue text alone does not single one of these out -- hydro, solar and wind are all renewable on the chapter's account, and question 11(c) of this same exercise names all three. What settles it is the printed grid, which allows only **four** letters at this clue.

**Green.**

Of electricity generated from water reservoirs, wind, sunlight and biofuels the chapter says: "electricity generation through these sources can be called environment friendly. We can also call the energy generated by these processes as green energy." The chapter is itself titled **Towards Green Energy**. The grid allows five letters.

**Kinetic.**

"The kinetic energy in wind has been used since long for lifting of water, for driving floor mill etc. The wind energy can also be used for electricity generation." The machine that does it is the wind turbine, "the machine which converts the kinetic energy of wind to electrical energy". The grid allows seven letters.

**Potential.**

"Kinetic energy in flowing water or the potential energy in water reservoir is a conventional source of energy. In hydroelectric power plant, the potential energy in water stored in dam is converted into kinetic energy of water." The grid allows nine letters.

[Textbook note: this chapter never defines either term. "Conventional" appears exactly once in it -- "Kinetic energy in flowing water or the potential energy in water reservoir is a conventional source of energy" -- and "non-conventional" appears nowhere in the chapter at all, only inside this exercise question. The answer below is therefore built from what the chapter does supply, and the one classification the chapter states outright is flagged, because it is easy to get backwards.]

The distinction the chapter's material supports is **how long a source has been in established large-scale use**, not whether it is renewable:

| Conventional sources | Non-conventional sources |
|---|---|
| In long-established, large-scale use for generation | Newer sources, being taken up as the world moves "towards green energy" |
| Coal, natural gas, petroleum, nuclear fuel, and -- on this chapter's own wording -- the water reservoir of a hydroelectric plant | Sunlight (photovoltaic and solar thermal), wind, biofuels |
| Together they carry most of the load: coal alone is 60 per cent of India's generation and 41 per cent of the world's | Together 15.7 per cent in India and 6 per cent in the world, on the chapter's table |

**The point to be careful about:** the chapter calls the potential energy of a water reservoir **a conventional source**, even though elsewhere it treats hydroelectricity as perpetual, environment friendly and a form of green energy. So on this chapter's account "conventional" and "non-renewable" are **not** the same idea -- hydro is conventional and renewable at once. The renewable/non-renewable split is about whether the source is exhaustible; the conventional/non-conventional split is about how long it has been in ordinary use.

Both plants generate electricity in the same way, and differ only in where the heat comes from.

**What is the same.** In each, thermal energy is used to raise steam of high temperature and pressure; the steam drives a turbine; the turbine drives a generator; the generator produces electricity by electromagnetic induction; the spent steam is condensed back to water and re-circulated. The tail of the two energy chains is identical: Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy.

**What differs.**

| Thermal electricity generation | Solar thermal electricity generation |
|---|---|
| Heat from **burning coal** in a boiler | Heat from **concentrated sunlight**: "many reflectors reflect and concentrate solar radiation on absorbers. There solar energy is converted into heat energy" |
| Chain begins Chemical energy in coal \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy | Chain begins Solar energy \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy |
| A fuel is consumed, so burning emits carbon dioxide, sulphur oxide, nitrogen oxide and soot | No fuel is burnt, so none of that combustion pollution arises |
| Coal reserves "are limited" and will run short in future | Sunlight is among the sources the chapter calls "never-ending i.e are perpetual" |
| Can run at any hour | Depends on sunshine being available |

In the chapter's own terms the first is not environment friendly, while the second is a green energy technology.

**Green energy** is the chapter's name for energy generated in ways that avoid the problems of fossil and nuclear fuels. Having listed those problems it says: "There are other ways of electricity production which avoids above problems. Electricity generation from water reservoir, wind, sunlight, biofuels etc. are the examples of such methods... Therefore, electricity generation through these sources can be called environment friendly. We can also call the energy generated by these processes as green energy."

A source qualifies on **two** counts, both of which the chapter states:

1. **It is perpetual.** "The energy sources used in such options i.e. water-reservoir, wind, sunlight, biofuel are never-ending i.e are perpetual" -- unlike coal, natural gas and petroleum, which "took millions of years" to form and whose reserves are limited.
2. **Using it does not damage the environment.** "Moreover, use of these sources do not lead to environmental problems discussed above" -- no combustion gases, no soot, no radioactive waste.

**Examples given by the chapter:** the water reservoir (hydroelectric power), wind (wind turbines), sunlight (solar photovoltaic cells and solar thermal plants) and biofuels.

The chapter is honest that this is not perfectly clean-cut: of hydroelectricity it notes the submerging of villages, forests and fertile land and the effect on river life, and says "it has always been a point of debate whether the hydroelectricity is environment friendly or not".

Energy from fossil fuels fails **both** of the tests the chapter sets for green energy.

**It damages the environment.** "Burning of fossil fuels like coal, and natural gas leads to emission of certain gases and soot particles. This results in air pollution." The chapter is specific: incomplete combustion forms carbon monoxide, which "adversely affects our health"; the rising percentage of carbon dioxide "affects environment severely", of which "the phenomena of global warming is an example"; nitrogen dioxide from burning coal, diesel and petrol "leads to problems like acid-rain"; and soot particles "can lead to problems related to respiratory system, like asthma".

**Its source is not perpetual.** "It took millions of years for formation of fossil fuels like coal, crude oils and natural gases (LPG and CNG). Also, the reserves of these fuels are limited. They are going to deplete in future." At the current rate of use the chapter puts the world's coal at about 200 years and natural gas at about 200 to 300 years.

Green energy requires a source that is "never-ending i.e. perpetual" **and** whose use "does not lead to environmental problems". Fossil fuels satisfy neither, so the chapter concludes plainly that "the energy generation from fossil fuels and nuclear fuels are not environment friendly".

The chapter's closing advice is exactly this: "Though use of energy is unavoidable in our day to day life, it is necessary to use it carefully and only in the required amount." Two reasons from the chapter make it urgent.

**The fuels we mostly use are running out.** Most electricity still comes from fossil fuels -- on the chapter's table, coal alone is 60 per cent of India's generation and 41 per cent of the world's. But these "took millions of years" to form, "the reserves of these fuels are limited", and at present rates of use the chapter gives the world's coal about 200 years and its natural gas about 200 to 300 years. Every unit saved is a unit of a finite stock left for later.

**Generating it damages the environment.** Because that electricity is mostly produced by burning coal and gas, using less of it directly means less carbon dioxide, sulphur oxide, nitrogen oxide and soot -- and so less global warming, acid rain and respiratory illness. Where the electricity is nuclear, using less also means less nuclear waste to dispose of safely.

Saving energy is thus the cheapest available way of doing both things at once: extending the life of limited reserves and reducing pollution, while green energy sources are being built up.

By connecting panels in **series** and in **parallel** in the right numbers -- the same two rules the chapter gives for cells.

- **Series raises the potential difference.** "If two solar cells are connected in series... the potential difference obtained from this combination is addition of the potential differences of individual solar cells. However, the current generated from this combination is equal to the current from an individual cell."
- **Parallel raises the current.** "If two solar cells are connected in parallel, the current generated from this combination is the summation of the currents from an individual solar cells. However, the potential difference obtained from this combination is the same as the potential difference obtained from individual cell."

The chapter builds a hierarchy on these two rules: "solar cell is the basic unit in solar electric plant. Many solar cells come together to form a solar panel. Many solar panels connected in series form a solar strings, and, many solar strings connected in parallel form a solar array."

So, to obtain a required output: connect enough panels **in series** to reach the potential difference wanted -- that is one string -- and then connect enough such **strings in parallel** to reach the current wanted, giving a solar array. Since panels may be added in either direction without limit, "we can obtain as much electrical power as needed", from the marginal power of a solar calculator up to "power station of MW capacity".

**Advantages**

- **No pollution from combustion.** "In this way, electricity is generated without any fuel combustion and so without any air pollution" -- no carbon dioxide, sulphur oxide, nitrogen oxide or soot, and no nuclear waste.
- **A perpetual source.** Sunlight is one of the sources the chapter calls "never-ending i.e are perpetual", so unlike coal or natural gas it cannot be exhausted.
- **Free choice of scale.** Because cells and panels can be combined in series and parallel, "we can obtain as much electrical power as needed"; the chapter's range runs from applications "which need marginal power (e.g. calculators that run on solar energy) to power station of MW capacity".
- **The fewest conversion steps.** A photovoltaic cell converts solar energy directly into electrical energy, "without using generator and without using the principle of electromagnetic induction".

**Limitations**

- **Day-time only.** "Since the energy is generated using solar radiation, solar cells can generate electricity during day-time only."
- **Storage is needed.** "Since the energy from solar cell is available only in presence of sunlight, the energy has to be stored in batteries for use at later time."
- **Low efficiency.** "A good solar cell can have an efficiency of around 15%. It means that if a solar panel receives power of 100 watt from solar radiation, the electrical power output from the panel will be 15 watt" -- so most of the sunlight falling on a panel is not converted.
- **The output is DC.** "Most of the equipment in domestic as well as industrial use run on AC power. In such case, the DC solar power must be converted to AC power using an electronic device called inverter."

The chapter adds one limitation for wind rather than solar, but of the same kind: a site must actually have the resource, and "the wind-velocity necessary for wind-energy generation is not available everywhere".

**Energy conversion in a thermal power plant** (the chapter's figure 5.6):

Chemical energy in coal \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy

**Step by step.**

1. **Chemical energy \(\rightarrow\) thermal energy.** Coal is burnt in the boiler; the chemical energy stored in it is released as heat.
2. **Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in steam.** That heat converts water in the boiler into "steam of very high temperature and pressure", so the heat now appears as energy of fast-moving steam.
3. **Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in turbine.** The steam is directed through a nozzle onto the blades of the steam turbine and makes it rotate: "when a flow of liquid or gas is directed on the blades of the turbine, it rotates... because of the kinetic energy of the flow".
4. **Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) electrical energy.** The turbine is coupled to the generator and rotates its magnet. By electromagnetic induction -- "whenever magnetic field around a conductor changes, a potential difference is generated across the conductor" -- electricity is produced.

The spent steam is then cooled back to water in the condenser, using water circulated from the cooling tower, and returned to the boiler.

[Textbook note: the chapter's cross-reference for this chart is wrong. On printed p50 the prose reads "The step-by-step transformation of energy is shown in figure 5.5", but figure 5.5 (printed p48) is the flow chart of the **thermal** power plant. The nuclear chart is the one printed immediately below that sentence, captioned "5.9 Energy transformation in nuclear power plant". Use figure 5.9.]

**Energy conversion in a nuclear power plant** (figure 5.9):

Nuclear energy \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy

**Step by step.**

1. **Nuclear energy \(\rightarrow\) thermal energy.** In the reactor, nuclei of Uranium or Plutonium undergo fission. A neutron striking a Uranium-235 nucleus makes Uranium-236, which "being extremely unstable converts into atoms of Barium and Krypton through a process of fission releasing three neutrons and 200 MeV energy". A controlled chain reaction keeps this going, and the energy appears as heat.
2. **Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in steam.** That heat is used "to generate the steam of high temperature and high pressure".
3. **Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in turbine.** "The energy in the steam rotates the turbine."
4. **Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) electrical energy.** The turbine "in turn drives the generator producing electricity" by electromagnetic induction.

As in the thermal plant, the steam is condensed back to water and re-circulated. The chapter's own summary of the chain is: "here nuclear energy is converted into thermal energy, thermal energy is converted into kinetic energy of steam, kinetic energy of steam is converted into kinetic energy of turbine and finally the kinetic energy of the turbine is converted into electrical energy".

The difference from the thermal plant is only in the first step: no fossil fuel is burnt, so "problems like air pollution do not arise" -- but the fission products are radioactive nuclear waste, and an accident can release very harmful radiations.

**Energy conversion in a solar thermal power plant:**

Solar energy \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy

**Step by step.**

1. **Solar energy \(\rightarrow\) thermal energy.** "Many reflectors reflect and concentrate solar radiation on absorbers. There solar energy is converted into heat energy."
2. **Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in steam.** "Using this heat energy steam is generated" -- water flowing through the absorber is turned to steam.
3. **Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in turbine.** The steam is led to the steam turbine and drives it.
4. **Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) electrical energy.** The turbine drives the electric generator, which produces electricity by electromagnetic induction; it is then fed to the power grid. The spent steam passes through a condenser served by a cooling tower and is pumped back.

From step 2 onwards this is exactly the thermal power plant. Only the first step differs: the heat comes from concentrated sunlight rather than from burning coal, so no fuel is consumed and no combustion gases or soot are produced.

**Note:** unlike the thermal, nuclear, natural-gas, hydroelectric and wind plants, the chapter prints no energy-form flow chart for this plant. Its figure 5.29 on printed p58 is a chain of **components** -- concentrators for collecting sunlight, absorber, steam turbine, electric generator, electric energy -- so the chain of energy forms above follows the pattern the chapter uses for its other thermal plants.

**Energy conversion in a hydroelectric power plant** (the chapter's figure 5.16):

Potential energy in water \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in flowing water \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy

**Step by step.**

1. **Potential energy \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy of water.** Water stored high in the dam has potential energy; when it is released down the penstock it speeds up, so "the potential energy in water stored in dam is converted into kinetic energy of water". The chapter notes the water is taken from about the middle of the dam's height.
2. **Kinetic energy of water \(\rightarrow\) kinetic energy in turbine.** "Fast flowing water is brought from the dam to the turbine at the bottom of the dam. The kinetic energy of the flowing water drives the turbine."
3. **Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) electrical energy.** "The turbine in turn drives the generator to generate electricity", again by electromagnetic induction.

This chain has one step fewer than the thermal and nuclear plants, because there is no fuel and no thermal stage at all -- which is why the chapter says "since no fuel is burnt in hydroelectric power generation, there is no pollution resulting from combustion of fuels".

Because **the turbine is driven by a different working fluid in each type of plant**, and each fluid arrives at a different pressure, temperature, density and speed.

The chapter states the fact and its cause together: "Based on which type of energy source is used to rotate the turbine, there are different types of power generating stations. The design of the turbine used in different types of power stations is also different."

The turbine works by having a flow directed onto its blades -- "when a flow of liquid or gas is directed on the blades of the turbine, it rotates... because of the kinetic energy of the flow". What that flow is varies:

- **Thermal, nuclear and solar thermal plants** use **steam** at very high temperature and pressure, delivered through a nozzle -- a **steam turbine**.
- **The natural-gas plant** uses **hot combustion gas** at very high temperature and pressure straight from the combustion chamber -- a **gas turbine**.
- **The hydroelectric plant** uses **fast-flowing water**, which is far denser and much slower than steam -- a **water turbine**.
- **The wind plant** uses **wind**, which is very much less dense again and slower still, so its turbine has long blades to sweep a large area, and the chapter notes it needs "a gear-box... to increase the rotations per unit time" before driving the generator.

Blades sized and shaped for high-pressure steam would be useless in air, and blades sized for wind would not survive steam -- hence a different construction for each.

Because the fission reaction **multiplies at every step**, and if left to itself the energy release would run away.

The chapter describes the mechanism: a neutron striking a Uranium-235 nucleus is absorbed, forming Uranium-236, which "being extremely unstable converts into atoms of Barium and Krypton through a process of fission releasing three neutrons and 200 MeV energy. The three neutrons generated in this process cause fission of three other Uranium-235 atoms releasing more energy." Those three fissions release nine neutrons, and so on -- this is what the chapter calls the **chain reaction**.

So one fission becomes three, three become nine, and the number of nuclei splitting, and with it the heat released, grows at every stage. What a power plant needs instead is a steady, predictable supply of heat to raise steam. Hence the chapter's wording: "In nuclear power plants, a **controlled** chain reaction results in release of thermal energy, which is used for electric energy generation."

The consequence of losing that control is severe, and the chapter says so among the problems of nuclear power: "An accident in nuclear power plant can be very fatal. This is because the accident may result in release of very harmful radiations."

Controlling the reaction therefore keeps the heat output matched to what the plant can use, and keeps the reactor and its radioactive contents safely contained.

Because their sources are **not used up** -- the chapter's term is "never-ending i.e are perpetual".

Contrast the two groups. Coal, natural gas, petroleum and nuclear fuel are drawn from a fixed stock: they "took millions of years" to form, "the reserves of these fuels are limited", and "they are going to deplete in future" -- the chapter gives the world's coal about 200 years and its natural gas about 200 to 300 years at current rates of use. Every tonne burnt is gone.

Hydro, solar and wind are different in kind:

- **Solar energy.** Sunlight falls on the earth day after day and generating electricity from it consumes nothing.
- **Wind energy.** Wind blows continually; a turbine takes kinetic energy from it without exhausting it.
- **Hydroelectric energy.** Water is not consumed either, and although a reservoir is drawn down as it generates, it refills: "although water reservoir is used for power generation, it can be replenished during rainy season leading to uninterrupted power generation."

Because the stock renews itself as fast as it is drawn on -- or is never depleted at all -- these are called **renewable** energies, and the chapter groups them with biofuels as the basis of green energy.

Because the **solar cell is a modular basic unit** whose output can be built up without limit by connecting more of them.

The chapter starts from a single cell: "a silicon solar cell of dimension 1 cm2 generates current of about 30 mA and potential difference of about 0.5 V" -- a very small amount of power, which is why a solar calculator needs only a few tiny cells.

Two rules then let that be scaled up in either direction independently. In **series** the potential differences add while the current stays the same; in **parallel** the currents add while the potential difference stays the same. The chapter's worked case: 36 cells of 100 cm2 in series give 18 V and 3 A.

Those combinations stack into a hierarchy: "solar cell is the basic unit in solar electric plant. Many solar cells come together to form a solar panel. Many solar panels connected in series form a solar strings, and, many solar strings connected in parallel form a solar array."

Since panels and strings may be added indefinitely, "as we can obtain as much electrical power as needed, they are used in applications which need marginal power (e.g. calculators that run on solar energy) to power station of MW capacity". The same technology therefore covers the whole range, from the very small outputs of a calculator up to megawatt power stations -- something no single large machine like a steam turbine could do, since a turbine cannot be scaled down to power a calculator.

**A note on the wording:** the chapter does not itself use the unit "mW" (milliwatt); its phrase for the small end of the range is "marginal power", illustrated by the solar calculator.

[Textbook note: two different figures in this chapter are both captioned **5.29** -- "Different stages in solar thermal power plant" on printed p58 and "Schematic of solar thermal power plant" on printed p59. The prose introducing the second one calls it "Figure 5.30", a number that is printed nowhere in the chapter, so the second figure should have been numbered 5.30. The schematic wanted here is the one on printed p59.]

**Schematic of solar thermal electric energy generation.** Draw and label these parts in this order, following the chapter's figure:

1. **Reflectors (concentrators)** -- a bank of mirrors spread out to catch sunlight, drawn with rays of solar energy falling on them and being turned towards a common line.
2. **Absorber** -- the pipe or trough at the focus of the reflectors, on which the concentrated sunlight falls. Label the incoming **solar energy** and the **flow of hot water** through it.
3. **Water inlet and steam outlet** -- water is fed to the absorber, is heated there, and leaves as **steam**. Label both.
4. **Steam turbine** -- the steam is piped to it and makes it rotate.
5. **Electric generator** -- shown coupled to the turbine shaft; this is where electricity is produced.
6. **Power grid** -- transmission towers taking the electrical energy away for distribution.
7. **Condenser and cooling tower** -- the steam leaving the turbine is condensed back to water, the cooling tower carrying the heat away.
8. **Pump** -- returning the condensed water to the absorber, closing the loop.

The chapter's summary of what the diagram shows: "many reflectors reflect and concentrate solar radiation on absorbers. There solar energy is converted into heat energy. Using this heat energy steam is generated to drive the turbine and generator."

From the steam onwards the diagram is the same as that of a thermal power plant; only the source of heat at the left-hand end is different.

The chapter puts this question to the reader itself, and gives both sides of it, saying that "it has always been a point of debate whether the hydroelectricity is environment friendly or not".

**The case that it is friendly**, from the chapter's list of advantages:

1. "Since no fuel is burnt in hydroelectric power generation, there is no pollution resulting from combustion of fuels" -- none of the carbon dioxide, sulphur oxide, nitrogen oxide or soot that a coal plant emits, and so no contribution to global warming or acid rain.
2. There is no radioactive waste and no risk of the kind of accident a nuclear plant carries.
3. The source is perpetual: the reservoir "can be replenished during rainy season leading to uninterrupted power generation", so nothing is depleted.
4. "If there is sufficient water storage in the dam, it is possible to generate electricity as and when necessary" -- unlike solar, which works only in daylight.

**The case against**, from the chapter's list of problems:

1. "The back-water due to storage of water in dam may submerge villages or towns in that area. This leads to the problems of rehabilitation of the displaced population." People lose their homes.
2. The same back-water "can also submerge forests as well as fertile land" -- a permanent loss of habitat and farmland.
3. "The obstruction of the flow of river water may have adverse effect on living world in the river."

**Opinion.** Judged on air pollution and on whether the source runs out, hydroelectric power is clearly environment friendly, and far better than a coal or nuclear plant. Judged on its effect on the land and the river it is not: submerging forests and fertile land and blocking a river damages the environment even though nothing is burnt, and displacing a community is a serious human cost besides. The fair conclusion is that it is environment friendly in the narrow sense the chapter uses for green energy -- a perpetual source with no combustion pollution -- but that it is not harmless, and each dam has to be judged on how much land and river life it costs against how much electricity it gives.

[Textbook note: the chapter prints an energy-form flow chart for the thermal (5.6), nuclear (5.9), natural-gas (5.13), hydroelectric (5.16) and wind (5.21) plants, but **not** for the solar thermal plant. Its figure 5.29 on printed p58 is a chain of components -- concentrators, absorber, steam turbine, electric generator -- not of energy forms. The diagram below therefore follows the pattern of the chapter's other thermal plants; it is not copied from a printed chart.]

**Energy transformation in solar thermal electric energy generation.** Draw five labelled boxes joined left to right by arrows:

Solar energy \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy

Label what happens at each arrow:

- **Solar energy \(\rightarrow\) Thermal energy** -- at the absorber, on which the reflectors concentrate the sunlight: "there solar energy is converted into heat energy".
- **Thermal energy \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in steam** -- in the absorber, where the heat turns water into high-pressure steam.
- **Kinetic energy in steam \(\rightarrow\) Kinetic energy in turbine** -- the steam strikes the blades of the steam turbine and rotates it.
- **Kinetic energy in turbine \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy** -- the turbine rotates the magnet of the generator, and electricity is produced by electromagnetic induction.

Note that the last four boxes are exactly those of the thermal power plant's chart (figure 5.6); only the first box differs, solar energy in place of the chemical energy in coal.

**Twelve panels: four in series, and three such strings in parallel.**

The two rules come from the chapter: connecting in **series** adds the potential differences while the current stays that of one unit, and connecting in **parallel** adds the currents while the potential difference stays that of one unit.

**Getting 72 V.** One panel gives 18 V, so panels must be put in series until the potential differences add to 72 V:

\(\text{number in series} = \dfrac{72\ \text{V}}{18\ \text{V}} = 4\)

Four panels in series give 72 V, and the current through them is still 3 A. In the chapter's vocabulary this run of panels in series is a **string**.

**Getting 9 A.** One such string gives 3 A, so strings must be put in parallel until the currents add to 9 A:

\(\text{number of strings in parallel} = \dfrac{9\ \text{A}}{3\ \text{A}} = 3\)

Three strings in parallel give 9 A, and the potential difference stays 72 V. Strings connected in parallel form a **solar array**, which is exactly what the question asks for.

**Total panels** \(= 4 \times 3 = 12\).

**The diagram.** Draw each panel as a battery symbol. Make three horizontal rows; in each row put four battery symbols end to end in series, so every row reads 72 V, 3 A. Then join the left-hand ends of the three rows to one another and the right-hand ends to one another, putting the rows in parallel. Mark the output terminals 72 V and 9 A.

**Check.** Each panel is 18 V and 3 A. Along a row the potential differences add (18 + 18 + 18 + 18 = 72 V) while the current stays 3 A. Across the three rows the currents add (3 + 3 + 3 = 9 A) while the potential difference stays 72 V. Both requirements are met.

**Electrical energy generation and environment**

Most of the world's electricity is still generated from fossil fuels and nuclear fuels. On the chapter's table of sources, coal supplies 41 per cent of the world's electricity and 60 per cent of India's, natural gas 22 and 08 per cent, nuclear energy 11 and 02, petroleum 04 and 0.3, hydroelectric 16 and 14, and renewable sources such as wind and solar 06 and 15.7 per cent. The chapter's judgement on the first group is blunt: "Electricity generation based on fossil fuels like coal, natural gas and nuclear fuels like uranium and plutonium are not environment friendly."

It gives three reasons.

**1. Air pollution.** Burning coal and natural gas emits gases and soot particles. Incomplete combustion forms carbon monoxide, which "adversely affects our health". The rising percentage of carbon dioxide "affects environment severely", and "the phenomena of global warming is an example of this". Nitrogen dioxide from burning coal, diesel and petrol "leads to problems like acid-rain". Soot particles "can lead to problems related to respiratory system, like asthma". Burning coal also releases sulphur oxide; the chapter notes that natural gas, containing no sulphur, pollutes less than coal.

**2. The fuels are finite.** Coal, crude oil and natural gas "took millions of years" to form and "the reserves of these fuels are limited. They are going to deplete in future." At present rates of use the chapter gives the world's coal about 200 years and its natural gas about 200 to 300 years.

**3. Nuclear waste and accidents.** The products left after fission "are also radioactive and emit harmful radiations", and "how to dispose the nuclear waste safely is a big challenge before the scientists". Further, "an accident in nuclear power plant can be very fatal", because it may release very harmful radiations.

**The way forward.** Because of this the chapter turns to generation "from water reservoir, wind, sunlight, biofuels etc.", whose sources "are never-ending i.e are perpetual" and whose "use... does not lead to environmental problems discussed above". Energy generated this way is called **green energy**, and "the world is now heading towards environment friendly energy i.e. green energy". Even so the chapter is careful not to call every alternative harmless -- it records that hydroelectric dams submerge villages, forests and fertile land and obstruct river life -- and it closes with the reminder that "though use of energy is unavoidable in our day to day life, it is necessary to use it carefully and only in the required amount".
